name: Uma Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't linked to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and nothing you say will carry your name. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Mehmet and I rent Low Fold from the Calder Estate, 120 hectares on the side of the hill. We rear dairy heifers for three big dairy farms, about 180 at any time, and grow potatoes and oats. I do the calves and the heifers, Mehmet does most of the tractor work. I'm out at six, in for breakfast at nine, out again until dark in winter.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like rearing a good heifer, sending her back to the dairy fit and calm. What wears me out is the forms, and I don't do computers. Our daughter Elif does the online cattle forms for me on Sunday nights. The other thing is the tenancy, which comes up for renewal in 2030, and the estate will want more rent, they always do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read the card as it's written. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, there you go, all that fuss. I don't go online, so it'd be at the auction mart over a cup of tea. I'd say it plainly and move on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it changes nothing, and nothing is fine. The worry I already have is the 2030 tenancy renewal. The Calder Estate put the rent up twelve percent last time, and I expect the same again in 2030.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on as we are. Put a bit more aside each month, so if the rent goes up in 2030 we can pay it without blinking. Mehmet wants to put away 300 a month, I'd say 500.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled, mostly. I just don't like waiting on the estate's letter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if the estate puts the rent up again?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd pay it. We've got good savings and the little rented bungalow in town that Mehmet's mother left us. I'd just be cross about it for a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would AI Plateau tempt you to try any of the new tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I'll leave that to the young ones. Elif's fine doing my forms, and I don't need a machine telling me when a heifer's bulling, I can see it.

say: I'd say **all that fuss** for nothing, over tea at the auction mart.
I'd say it **plainly** and move on.
think: AI changing nothing is **fine** by me.
The real worry is the **2030 tenancy** renewal and another rent rise.
do: Carry on rearing heifers and growing **potatoes and oats**.
Put **500 a month** aside to cover a rent rise in 2030.
feel: **Settled**, apart from waiting on the **estate's letter**.
S0.quote: The Calder Estate put the rent up twelve percent last time, and I expect the same again in 2030.
fieldNote: Her standing worry is the **tenancy**, not technology.
Has **solid backing**: savings plus a rented bungalow from Mehmet's mother.
Plainly refuses new tools and relies on her daughter **Elif** for forms.

steps.text: Keep rearing 180 heifers and growing potatoes and oats at Low Fold
Put 500 a month aside for the 2030 rent rise

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good luck to them, but a computer can't rear a heifer. At the mart I'd say the office types should be worried, not us. That's about as far as I'd go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the thing I'd watch is the estate. If their land agent's office uses AI to do the sums on every farm, they'll know to the penny what they can squeeze out of us in 2030. The farm work itself, I think, stays ours a good while yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as normal and see what the estate does. If the cattle forms move to some AI system, Elif would have to do even more of them for me, or teach Mehmet. I wouldn't buy anything new until I'd seen it work on three farms, not one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not panicky. Like when the forecast says rain for haymaking and you're not sure whether to cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Mehmet see it the same way?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mehmet would probably want to try something. He's always been a bit keener. I'd say fine, as long as it's his money and not the rent money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anyone in the family more exposed than you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our son Kerem works at a big parcel warehouse in town. They've already got robot arms there, so this one worries me for Kerem more than for us. I'd tell my son Kerem to get his forklift and electrical tickets while he's still got a job.

say: Good luck to them, but a computer **can't rear a heifer**.
The **office types** should be worried, not farmers like us at the mart.
think: The **land agent** could use AI to work out exactly how much rent to squeeze.
The **farm work** itself stays ours for a good while.
do: Carry on as normal and **watch the estate**.
Lean on **Elif** for any new AI cattle forms.
Buy nothing new until it works on **three farms**.
feel: **Uneasy**, like a doubtful forecast at **haymaking** time.
S1.quote: I'd tell my son Kerem to get his forklift and electrical tickets while he's still got a job.
fieldNote: Sees AI as a tool for the **landlord**, not for her.
Her son **Kerem** in a warehouse is the family member she worries about most.
Keeps a firm line between **rent money** and anything new.

steps.text: Wait to see what the Calder Estate's land agent does
Keep rearing heifers and growing potatoes as now
Ask Elif to handle any new AI cattle forms on Sundays

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going too fast and somebody in government should put the brakes on. I'm not one for marching, but I'd sign anything that slowed it down. At the mart, everyone would be saying the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Here's what I really think. The tenancy ends in 2030, and by then the estate's office would have AI telling them a robot can farm Low Fold cheaper than we pay in rent. The robots come in 2031, so they'd either not renew us or give us a short lease and wait. At 62 I'd lose the farm, our home and our income all in one letter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I'd save every penny for the next two years and not buy the new trailer. When AGI arrives in 2028, I'd ask the estate straight out what they plan, in writing. If they won't renew, we'd sell the heifers, retire early and move into Mehmet's mother's bungalow in town, which means giving the tenants there notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, if you want the honest word. I'd be lying awake doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would hurt most if the estate didn't renew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The house. People forget the farmhouse comes with the tenancy. Leaving that kitchen after twenty-six years would be worse than leaving the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd tell Elif and Kerem together, at Sunday dinner. Elif would want us to move near her, and Kerem would be worried about his own job. I'd tell my children we're not poor, we just won't be farmers.

say: It's going **too fast**, and the government should put the brakes on.
I'd **sign anything** that slowed it down, though I don't march.
think: The estate could choose **robots over tenants** when our lease ends in 2030.
At **62** we'd lose the farm, home and income in one letter.
do: Save every penny and **skip the new trailer** for two years.
Ask the estate **in writing** about renewal as soon as AGI arrives.
Sell the heifers and **move to the bungalow** if they won't renew.
feel: Dreads leaving the **farmhouse kitchen** most of all.
S2.quote: People forget the farmhouse comes with the tenancy.
fieldNote: The **2030 lease date** falls right in the gap between AGI and robots.
Expects to lose **farm, home and income** together, which drives her alarm.
Has a clear **fallback**: savings and the bungalow in town.

steps.text: Skip the new trailer and save every penny for two years
Sell the heifers and retire early if the lease isn't renewed
Move into the town bungalow after giving its tenants notice

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to sort it if people stop arguing and get on with it. Make rules for landlords, so tenants aren't just thrown off for a machine. I'd say that to the tenant farmers' association, which I've paid into for years and never been to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The renewal in 2030 comes a year before the AI, so I'd have a chance. If I can get a long lease signed before the estate's office starts doing its sums with AGI, we'd be safe until I'm ready to stop. The robots come about 2034, and I'm 66 then anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the tenant farmers' association meeting for the first time and ask them to push for longer leases. I'd ask the estate for a ten-year renewal in 2030 and offer a bit more rent to get it signed. And I'd keep the 500 a month going into savings, just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I've got something to do about it. That's better than the fast one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much would you offer to get the lease signed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd offer maybe eight percent more rather than wait for them to ask twelve. A long lease is worth the money. My husband Mehmet would say I'm giving the rent away, and I'd say I'm buying ten years of sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And if the estate won't give you ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then we'd do the same as in the fast one, just at 63 instead of 62. Sell up the stock, move to town. We'd have had a few years' warning, which makes it easier to swallow.

say: There's **time to sort it** if people stop arguing.
Landlords need **rules**, so tenants aren't thrown off for a machine.
think: The **2030 renewal** comes a year before AGI, so I'd have a chance.
A **long lease** signed early would carry us to retirement.
do: Go to the **tenant farmers'** association for the first time.
Offer about **eight percent** more rent for a ten-year lease.
Keep **500 a month** going into savings.
feel: **Worried**, but with **something to do** about it.
S3.quote: My husband Mehmet would say I'm giving the rent away, and I'd say I'm buying ten years of sleep.
fieldNote: The five-year warning lets her **get ahead** of the landlord's AI sums.
Shows **pragmatism**: pays more now to buy certainty.
Joins a group for the **first time**, which is out of character.

steps.text: Attend the tenant farmers' association and push for longer leases
Offer the estate eight percent more rent for a ten-year lease
Keep saving 500 a month in case the lease fails

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a long way off and I'll be long out of it. Let the young ones plan for it. That's what I'd say at the mart, and nobody would argue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's after my time. We'd renew in 2030, farm until I'm 66 or so, and hand the tenancy back. AGI in 2036 and robots in 2039 would be the next tenant's problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different, really. Renew the lease in 2030, keep rearing heifers, keep saving. Wait and see what the estate does after we're gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. A bit sad for whoever comes after, but fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the farm after you leave?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the bit I don't like. Low Fold has always had a family in the farmhouse, and a robot company might leave the house sitting empty. That's a waste of a good house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Kerem he's got ten years to get out of that warehouse and into something with a person in it. I'd tell Elif to keep doing whatever she's doing, she's sensible.

say: It's a **long way off**, and I'll be out of it.
Let the **young ones** plan for it.
think: We'd renew in **2030** and farm until about 66.
**AGI and robots** would be the next tenant's problem.
do: Renew the **lease** in 2030 and keep rearing heifers.
Keep **saving** and wait to see the estate's plans.
feel: **Fine**, with some sadness for **whoever comes after**.
S4.quote: Low Fold has always had a family in the farmhouse, and a robot company might leave the house sitting empty.
fieldNote: The ten-year warning puts robots well **after her retirement**.
Her remaining unease is about the **farmhouse** and the estate, not her income.
Still pushes her son **Kerem** to leave the warehouse.

steps.text: Renew the Low Fold lease in 2030 and keep rearing heifers
Wait to see what the estate plans after they leave

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, AGI by 2028, because our lease runs out right in the middle of it. What would help is a law that a tenant farmer gets first refusal on a long lease, and can't be put out just because a machine is cheaper. That, and fair notice.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about tenants. Everybody talks about farmers like we all own the land. Half the farmers I know rent, and a tenant can lose everything with one letter from the landlord.

headlineQuote: Half the farmers I know rent, and a tenant can lose everything with one letter from the landlord.
portrait: A 58-year-old **tenant farmer** rearing dairy heifers at Low Fold with her husband Mehmet.
Never uses AI; her daughter **Elif** fills in the online forms on Sunday nights.
Her fears centre on the **2030 lease renewal** and the landlord's choices.
Has a solid **cushion** of savings and a rented bungalow in town.
**Alarmed** if AGI comes in 2028, uneasy or anxious when there's warning to sign a lease.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because her lease ends in the middle of it.
whatWouldHelp: A law giving tenants **first refusal** on a long lease.
**Fair notice** before a landlord swaps tenants for machines.
